findings.title: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never true for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed
findings.body: `_ensure_processes_alive` now only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The flusher processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which returns `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.Process` (`multiprocessing.context.Process`), so the check is always False in production and the kill is silently skipped. Consequences: for the `hang` cause, a new process is started for the same shards while the old one is left running; when the old process unblocks (e.g. Kafka/Redis recovers) two processes flush the same shards concurrently and both produce the same segments to buffered-segments (duplicates), and each restart leaks a process plus its Redis connection and KafkaProducer (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per index). The previous code called `kill()` unconditionally, so this is a regression introduced by the guard. Use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)` (or `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`), and add a test for the restart path, which currently has no coverage.

findings.title: join() never terminates spawn processes and skips cleanup of remaining processes after deadline
findings.body: In `join`, `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()` has the same problem as the kill path: `SpawnProcess` is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`, so `terminate()` is never invoked. Additionally the loop `break`s as soon as the deadline has passed, so any processes after the first one in iteration order are neither waited on nor terminated. Shutdown therefore relies entirely on the `stopped` flag and `daemon=True`; a process stuck in `future.result()` or a Redis call will not be stopped by `join` and will only die when the parent exits.

findings.title: `time.sleep(0.1)` added to fix a race is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched earlier in the same test
findings.body: `test_basic` starts with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` and then later calls `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change". Because the test references `time.sleep` through the module attribute, it resolves to the patched lambda and returns immediately, so no time is actually given. The race the comment describes (flusher thread must observe `current_drift = 9000` and flush before `step.join()` sets `stopped`) is unchanged, and the test remains timing-dependent/flaky. Bind the real sleep before patching (as `test_flusher.py` does with `from time import sleep`) or wait on an explicit condition (e.g. poll until `messages` is non-empty).

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key (`shard` vs `shards`) and comma-joined shard list used as a tag value
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `{"shard": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `{"shards": shard_tag}` for the same value, so the three metrics cannot be grouped/filtered by the same tag key in dashboards. Also `shard_tag` is `",".join(shards)`; with the CLI default of one flusher process this becomes a value like `0,1,2,...,31`. Commas are the tag separator in the statsd/DogStatsD wire format and are either mangled by the client or split into bogus tags, and the set of possible combinations changes with every rebalance, creating unbounded tag cardinality. Prefer a stable key and either a per-process index tag or per-shard emission.

findings.title: Redis memory info is fetched once per flusher process and summed, duplicating cluster-wide data
findings.body: `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info()` reports Redis node memory via `INFO memory` on every node of the cluster; it is not shard-scoped. Iterating `self.buffers.values()` and extending `memory_infos` therefore issues the same INFO calls N times (N = number of flusher processes) and sums N copies of `used` and `available` on every `submit()` when `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage < 1.0`. The ratio happens to come out the same, but the Redis round trips scale with process count for no benefit. Similarly `record_stored_segments()` is now N pipeline round trips instead of one. Keeping the original full-shard `buffer` on `self` for these two calls avoids the duplication.

findings.title: Docstring claims one process per shard; actual behaviour depends on `max_processes` with a CLI default of 1 and a `None` default of per-shard
findings.body: The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but `SpanFlusher` creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes with shards distributed round-robin, and the `process-spans` CLI option defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so in production the default is a single process handling all shards. Conversely, constructing `SpanFlusher`/`ProcessSpansStrategyFactory` directly with `flusher_processes=None` (or `0`, because of `max_processes or len(...)`) silently spawns one Django-initialized process per assigned shard, which for consumers with many partitions can be dozens of processes. The docstring should describe the real mapping and document the `max_processes` parameter (the existing `:param topic:` also refers to a parameter that does not exist).

findings.title: `--flusher-processes` accepts 0 and negative values with surprising results
findings.body: The new `--flusher-processes` option is a plain `int` with no range validation and help text "Defaults to 1". Passing `0` is treated as falsy by `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and results in one process per shard rather than zero or an error. Passing a negative value makes `num_processes` negative, `process_to_shards_map` empty, and `i % num_processes` evaluate to 0 (or negative), so `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index]` raises `KeyError` during `create_with_partitions`, i.e. the consumer crashes on partition assignment with an unhelpful error. Use `click.IntRange(min=1)` or validate in the factory.

findings.title: New multi-process test only checks counts; no test exercises flushing across multiple processes or the restart path
findings.body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2` and that the total shard count is 4, then joins. It never submits spans, so nothing verifies that segments on shards handled by the second process are actually flushed, that each shard is assigned to exactly one process (a shard appearing twice would still satisfy the sum check), or that per-process backpressure/health values propagate to `submit()`. `_ensure_processes_alive` (unhealthy detection, kill, re-spawn, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS) is also untested, which is how the non-functional `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard went unnoticed.

findings.title: `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the module or elsewhere in the diff; restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly from `_ensure_processes_alive`. Dead helpers that look like public-ish API on the strategy add maintenance burden and can mislead future callers (it does not kill the existing process before starting a new one, so calling it would double up flushers for those shards). Remove it or wire it in with the kill logic.

findings.title: Unrelated documentation change bundled into the flusher refactor
findings.body: The PR adds a new `hasattr()` vs `isinstance()` anti-pattern section to `CLAUDE.md`. This has nothing to do with the span-buffer flusher change described in the PR title/description and is not mentioned there. Mixing unrelated guidance edits into a behavioural consumer change makes the commit harder to review and revert; it should be split into its own PR.
